title: Calling It In: Microbiology Critical Results, Corrections and Early Warning
summary: Learn what a complete microbiology record holds, how critical results are called with read-back and documentation, how a wrong released result is corrected openly, how the laboratory warns infection prevention and public health, and why only validated negatives are released automatically.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 66 Hits 41–44 and Trap 8. Record, critical-alert and corrected-report duties from US CLIA text (42 CFR 493.1241, 493.1283, 493.1291; eCFR version 2026-10-01); critical-list practice from Croatian national recommendations and Portuguese and international surveys; early-warning role from Cantón 2005, Mencacci 2023 and the CDC NNDSS page; autoverification from Burckhardt 2018 and Mencacci 2023. The reviewer’s fixed critical list (CSF Gram stain, blood cultures, AFB smear, malaria smear) is taught as examples of lab-defined lists (register flag rv-micro-critical-list-local); regulatory and reportable-disease content is US-only (rv-micro-reporting-us-law). Not taught as fact: chain-of-custody requirements, documenting the collector’s identity, select-agent reporting rules.

objectives: List what US rules require on a laboratory request, record and report, and how that applies to a microbiology result.
Describe how a critical microbiology result is communicated and documented, and why critical lists are laboratory-defined.
State the steps for correcting a released result, and the laboratory’s early-warning duties to infection prevention and public health.
Explain which microbiology results can be released automatically and why results with growth still need a technologist.

scenes.title: Four results, one night shift
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: on one night shift a microbiology technologist has (1) bacteria seen on a cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) Gram stain, (2) a urine culture report released yesterday that named the wrong organism, (3) the third carbapenem-resistant isolate this week from the same ward, and (4) a stack of culture plates that an imaging system has sorted as “negative”. Question token: “Who must hear, and how?”

cues.text: One night shift, four problems: bacteria on a spinal fluid Gram stain, and a urine report released yesterday that named the wrong organism.
There is also a third carbapenem-resistant isolate this week from the same ward, and a stack of plates an imaging system has sorted as negative.
Who must hear about each one, and how?

scenes.title: What a complete record holds
scenes.altText: Three schematic cards based on US CLIA regulation text. Requisition card (42 CFR 493.1241(c)): patient name or unique identifier; sex and age or date of birth; test requested; specimen source when appropriate; date and, if appropriate, time of collection; a contact for urgent results. Record card (493.1283): positive specimen identification; date and time received in the laboratory; condition and disposition of unacceptable specimens; dates of testing and identity of the person who tested. Report card (493.1291(c)): patient identification; testing laboratory name and address; report date; test performed; specimen source when appropriate; result with units or interpretation; condition of any unacceptable specimen. In microbiology the reported result typically includes the organism identified and, when tested, its susceptibility results (Buehler et al., 2016 describe reporting of identification and susceptibility results).

cues.text: A microbiology result is only as good as its record. Under US rules, the request form must ask for the patient identifier, sex and age or date of birth, the test, the specimen source where appropriate, the collection date and, when relevant, the time.
The laboratory record adds positive specimen identification, when the specimen arrived, what happened to any unacceptable specimen, and who did the testing and when.
The report itself states the patient, the laboratory, the report date, the test, the source, and the result with its interpretation.
In microbiology the result usually names the organism identified and, when tested, its susceptibility results.

scenes.title: Critical results: call, read back, record
scenes.altText: Rule card (CLIA 493.1291(g)): the laboratory must IMMEDIATELY alert the person who ordered the test, or who uses the result, when a result indicates an imminently life-threatening condition or a panic/alert value. List card: each laboratory defines its own critical-result list, in consultation with the clinicians it serves (Croatian national recommendations, 2019). Examples found in published lists and surveys: pathogenic bacteria on a CSF Gram stain and malaria parasites (Croatian list); the Gram stain of a positive blood culture (reported as a critical value in studies reviewed by Buehler et al., 2016); acid-fast bacilli, the microbiology critical result most often listed in a Portuguese survey (23 of 26 laboratories). Procedure card (Croatian recommendations): report verbally to authorised staff, have the receiver read the result back, follow with a written or electronic report, and record who reported, who received, the channel and the time; one national target is within 30 minutes of confirmation. Surveys show read-back is practised inconsistently between countries.

cues.text: Some results cannot wait in the computer. US CLIA rules require the laboratory to alert the ordering clinician immediately when a result signals an imminently life-threatening condition.

Each laboratory writes its own critical list with its clinicians. Published lists include bacteria on a spinal fluid Gram stain, malaria parasites, the Gram stain of a positive blood culture, and acid-fast bacilli, the microbiology result most often listed in one national survey.
The call goes to an authorised person, who reads the result back. Then the laboratory records who called, who received it, how, and when, and follows with the written report.
One national guideline asks for the call within thirty minutes of confirmation. Surveys show read-back is still practised unevenly from country to country.

scenes.title: Corrections and the early-warning role
scenes.altText: Correction card (CLIA 493.1291(k)): when an error in a reported result is detected, promptly notify the ordering clinician, promptly issue a corrected report, and keep duplicates of BOTH the original and the corrected report. Surveillance card: laboratory software should flag unusual results, rising trends and accumulating cases (Cantón, 2005); timely reporting of multidrug-resistant organisms lets the hospital start contact precautions and investigate clusters (Mencacci et al., 2023). Public-health card (CDC): in the US each state or territory decides by law which diseases must be reported, and laboratories must tell the health department. Hook answer card: (1) call the CSF Gram stain now with read-back and documentation; (2) notify, issue a corrected urine report, keep the original; (3) alert infection prevention to the cluster, and report to public health if the condition is reportable locally; (4) negatives may be auto-released only under a validated rule.

cues.text: When a released result turns out to be wrong, US rules require three things: promptly tell the ordering clinician, promptly issue a corrected report, and keep both the original and the corrected version.

The laboratory is also an early-warning post. Its software should flag unusual results, rising trends and clusters, and fast reporting of resistant organisms lets the hospital start contact precautions and investigate.
Some findings must leave the hospital. In the United States, state and territorial laws list the reportable diseases, and laboratories must tell the health department.

Back to the hook: call the spinal fluid Gram stain now, with read-back. Correct the urine report openly and keep the original. Alert infection prevention to the cluster. And release negatives automatically only under a validated rule.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Microbiology cultures autoverify like chemistry results” (✓ validated automated imaging can release negative plates, with high sensitivity and negative predictive value in published studies, but its specificity and positive predictive value for growth are lower, so plates it flags as growth are read by a technologist); “Silently overwrite a wrong released result” (✓ notify, corrected report, keep the original); “A critical result posted in the system has been communicated” (✓ alert a person directly, read-back, document).

cues.text: Trap one: cultures autoverify like chemistry. Not quite: a validated imaging system can release negative plates, but many of its growth calls are false alarms, so plates it flags as growth go to a technologist.
Trap two: quietly fix a wrong released result. No: notify the clinician, issue a corrected report, and keep the original.
Trap three: a critical result posted in the system has been communicated. No: alert a person directly, ask for read-back, and document it.

props.title: ✗ “Cultures autoverify like chemistry.”
lines: ✓ Validated negatives only; flagged growth → technologist

props.title: ✗ “It’s in the system, so it’s communicated.”

scenes.title: Ring, repeat, record
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “RING, REPEAT, RECORD for a critical result: ring a real person, have them repeat it back, record who, whom and when. And FIX IN THE OPEN: a correction is a new, visible report, never an eraser.” Tokens: Ring · Repeat · Record · Fix in the open. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: ring, repeat, record. Ring a real person, have them repeat it back, and record who, whom and when. And fix in the open: a correction is a new, visible report, never an eraser.
Where it breaks: critical lists, timing and read-back rules are set locally; some systems deliver alerts electronically with receipt confirmation; and reportable-disease lists differ by jurisdiction.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Complete record · critical result = call + read-back + documentation · corrected report keeps the original”, “Flag clusters to infection prevention · report as local law requires · auto-release only validated negatives”.

cues.text: A microbiology result is finished only when it is completely recorded, critical results are called to a person who reads them back, corrections are issued openly with the original kept, clusters reach infection prevention, and only validated negatives are released automatically.

props.label: Complete record · call + read-back · corrected report keeps original
Clusters → infection prevention · validated negatives only auto-release

explanation.what: Plain language: a microbiology result needs a complete paper trail; life-threatening results are phoned to a real person who repeats them back; mistakes are fixed with a new visible report, not erased; the laboratory warns infection prevention about resistant organisms and clusters and tells public health about reportable diseases; and computers may release only negatives that a validated system has confirmed. Scientific terms: requisition, positive specimen identification, critical (panic/alert) result, read-back, corrected report, multidrug-resistant organism (MDRO), surveillance, notifiable/reportable disease, autoverification, automated plate imaging.
explanation.why: A result that does not reach the right person in time cannot change care; an erased error hides what the clinician may already have acted on; microbiology laboratories are first in line to detect emerging problems; and in published studies automated readers rarely miss growth but many of their growth calls are false (VRE plates: 100% sensitivity, 38% positive predictive value), so flagged plates need a technologist.
explanation.measure: US CLIA: request content (493.1241(c)); record content (493.1283); report content (493.1291(c)); immediate alert (493.1291(g)); corrections: notify, corrected report, keep original and corrected (493.1291(k)). Croatian recommendation: critical result reported within 30 minutes of confirmation, read back, documented. Survey data: read-back 46% (France, Australasia) vs 79% (UK); AFB most-listed micro critical result in Portugal (23/26). Automated reading: VRE plates 100% sensitivity and NPV, with 89% specificity and 38% positive predictive value; urine 97–99% sensitivity, 85–94% specificity in one system.
explanation.differs: Critical call (person, read-back, documentation) vs routine electronic release; corrected report (original kept) vs overwrite; infection-prevention alert (inside the hospital) vs public-health report (required by local law); auto-release of validated negatives vs technologist review of any growth.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the right action for a positive CSF Gram stain or blood culture, the steps after a wrong released result, who to alert about an MDRO cluster, and whether a microbiology culture result can be autoverified.

mnemonic.text: RING, REPEAT, RECORD for a critical result: ring a real person, have them repeat it back, record who, whom and when. And FIX IN THE OPEN: a correction is a new, visible report, never an eraser.
mnemonic.explanation: Ring = immediate direct alert; Repeat = read-back; Record = documentation; Fix in the open = notify, corrected report, keep the original.
mnemonic.limitation: Critical lists, timing and read-back rules are local policy; some systems deliver alerts electronically with receipt confirmation; reportable-disease lists differ by jurisdiction.

analogyLimitations: Cards are schematic; real LIS screens and critical lists are laboratory-specific.
Regulatory text paraphrased (US CLIA only); read the current regulation for exact wording.
takeaway: A microbiology result is finished only when it is completely recorded, critical results are called to a person who reads them back, corrections are issued openly with the original kept, clusters reach infection prevention, and only validated negatives are released automatically.

questions.stem: A technologist sees gram-negative diplococci on a CSF Gram stain at 02:00. Which action best meets critical-result practice?

options.text: Phone the responsible clinician now, have them read the result back, and document who received it and when
options.rationale: Correct. A result signalling an imminently life-threatening condition needs an immediate alert (CLIA 493.1291(g)); read-back guards against misunderstanding, and documentation records who received it and when.

options.text: Release the result in the LIS and let the ward see it on morning rounds
options.rationale: Incorrect. Posting a result is not an immediate alert to a person.

options.text: Wait for the culture to grow so the organism can be confirmed first
options.rationale: Incorrect. Bacteria on a CSF Gram stain are themselves on published critical lists, and waiting for confirmation only delays the call.

options.text: Leave a message with the ward clerk without recording the call
options.rationale: Incorrect. The call should go to an authorised person, be read back, and be documented.

questions.stem: A urine culture report released yesterday named the wrong organism. Under US CLIA, what must the laboratory do?

options.text: Edit the released report so it shows the right organism
options.rationale: Incorrect. A silent edit hides the error from a clinician who may already have acted on it, and the original must be kept.

options.text: Promptly notify the ordering clinician, issue a corrected report, and keep both the original and corrected reports
options.rationale: Correct. These are the three duties in 42 CFR 493.1291(k).

options.text: Delete the report and release a new one as if it were the first
options.rationale: Incorrect. Deleting removes the original, which must be kept with the corrected report.

options.text: Correct it only if the clinician asks about it
options.rationale: Incorrect. The laboratory must notify promptly on its own.

questions.stem: A laboratory uses a validated automated imaging system on its culture plates. Which result is the most suitable for automatic release without technologist review?

options.text: An MRSA screening plate the system flags as showing growth
options.rationale: Incorrect. Many growth calls by automated readers are false alarms (lower specificity and positive predictive value), so flagged plates need a technologist.

options.text: A positive blood culture with gram-positive cocci on Gram stain
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is a critical result that needs a direct call, not automatic release.

options.text: A urine culture plate the system classes as negative after the defined incubation time
options.rationale: Correct. Published studies show high sensitivity and negative predictive value, so plates a validated system calls negative can be reported without further human review.

options.text: A wound culture with three organisms growing
options.rationale: Incorrect. The evidence supports automatic release of negatives only; a plate with growth needs a technologist’s reading.

references.usedFor: Microbiology laboratories are first in line to detect emerging problems and act as sentinels; laboratory software should automatically alert unusual results and detect rising trends and accumulation of cases; data feed regional/national surveillance and notifiable-disease collection.

references.usedFor: Each US state or territory sets the laws listing reportable diseases; laboratories and other providers must tell public health departments; states voluntarily inform CDC.

claims.text: Required request, record and report content under US CLIA; microbiology results include organism identification and susceptibility results.
Immediate alert for imminently life-threatening or panic/alert results.
Critical lists are laboratory-defined with clinicians; examples (CSF Gram stain bacteria, malaria parasites, positive blood culture Gram stain, acid-fast bacilli).
Read-back, documentation of the call, written follow-up; 30-minute target in one national recommendation; read-back practised inconsistently.

Laboratory as early warning: alerts for unusual results, trends and clusters; MDRO reporting enables contact precautions and cluster investigation; US reportable diseases set by state/territorial law with laboratory reporting duty.
Automated reading: high sensitivity/NPV allows release of negatives; lower specificity means growth needs review.

Chain of custody for forensic/legal specimens; documenting the collector’s identity; select-agent and tuberculosis reporting specifics; the reviewer’s statement that micro positives never autoverify; colony count and collector identity as mandatory report elements.
claims.note: Not taught as facts in this lesson; no open source read in this session covers them.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer gives a fixed list of microbiology critical values (positive CSF Gram stain, positive blood cultures, positive AFB smear, positive malaria smear). Published recommendations and surveys show critical lists are defined by each laboratory with its clinicians and vary between laboratories; malaria parasites appear on haematology lists in some schemes. The lesson teaches these as examples, not a universal list.

The record, critical-alert and corrected-report duties and reportable-disease rules taught here are US federal (CLIA) and US state/territorial requirements. Philippine rules are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.

morphology.note: No images; records and alerts shown as schematic cards.
